title: Understanding Inner Conflict: More Harmony Through Working With Your Inner Parts
excerpt: One part of you wants change, another wants safety. The Internal Family Systems model offers a kind way to understand these inner tugs-of-war and ease the blocks they create.

value.text: There is a familiar kind of stuckness that has nothing to do with laziness or lack of insight. You know what you want to do. You have thought it through, perhaps for years. And still something in you pulls the handbrake. One part of you drafts the resignation letter; another remembers what security cost your family to build. One part longs to be close; another knows exactly what closeness can cost.

When two genuine wants sit in opposition, the usual response is to try to win the argument — to decide which side is the real you and overrule the other. It rarely works, because the overruled side does not actually leave. It goes underground and returns as procrastination, irritability, a tight chest, a decision endlessly deferred. The Internal Family Systems model, developed in the 1980s by the American family systems researcher Richard Schwartz, offers a kinder and more workable way to understand what is happening. I draw on its ideas as one of the approaches informing my counselling, not as a packaged method.
The inner tug-of-war, and what it quietly costs

IFS begins from an idea most people recognise the moment it is named: inwardly we are not one unified voice but something closer to an ensemble. There is a part that pushes and performs. A part that scans for disapproval. A part that wants to disappear when a room turns tense. A part that keeps you funny when a conversation gets too close. Everyday language already works this way — part of me wants to go, part of me wants to stay.

The cost of an unresolved inner conflict is rarely dramatic. It shows up as a low, constant drain: energy spent holding two positions at once, decisions revisited nightly, a background hum of self-criticism. Many people describe a tiredness that sleep does not touch. Nothing is exactly wrong, and nothing is exactly right either. This is often what sits underneath the gap between [functioning well and feeling well](/blog/functioning-well-vs-feeling-well).
Every part is trying to protect something

The model's most important premise — the one that changes the whole atmosphere of the enquiry — is that no part of you is trying to sabotage you. The inner critic that dismantles your work before anyone else can is trying to protect you from humiliation. The part that keeps you working late is protecting you from being seen as replaceable. The part that shuts down halfway through an argument learned, somewhere, that shutting down was safer than escalating.

These are strategies, and they were usually intelligent when they formed. The trouble is that they were designed for an earlier situation and never updated: a strategy that kept a fourteen-year-old safe may still be running a forty-year-old's marriage. Understanding a pattern as outdated protection rather than personal failure changes what becomes possible with it, because you can negotiate with a protector but not with a character flaw.
Listening for the need beneath the part
Working with parts is less like management and more like a conversation you have not had before. In plain terms it tends to move like this:

items: Notice the part as something you have rather than something you are — "a part of me feels..." instead of "I am...".
Locate it in the body if you can: the jaw, the chest, the stomach. Parts are often physical before they become verbal.
Ask what it is afraid would happen if it stopped doing its job.
Listen for the need underneath the behaviour — safety, recognition, belonging, rest.
Ask what would help it trust that the need can be met in another way.

value.text: That last question is usually where the movement happens. A part rarely steps back because it has been argued with; it steps back when it believes something else is looking after the thing it was guarding. Because this work travels through the body as much as through words, it sits well alongside [somatic experiencing](/work-with-me/somatic-experiencing), where physical sensation is the main doorway in.

Self-compassion is the working condition here rather than the reward. A part that feels judged will defend itself; a part that feels heard will usually soften. If you meet your own inner critic with contempt, you have merely added a second critic to the room. This is not the same as approving of everything you do — you can see clearly that a pattern is costing you and still be curious rather than punitive about why it exists.
A part that is fought will dig in. A part that is understood will usually make room.
Inner leadership: someone has to chair the meeting

IFS also describes a calmer, wider perspective that is not itself one of the parts — the you that can hear several of them at once without being taken over by any single one. People who find their way into it tend to describe the same thing: not certainty, but spaciousness. Room enough to hold two conflicting wants without collapsing into either.

That is what I mean by inner leadership, and building it is much of what we do together in [psychological counselling](/work-with-me/psychological-counselling). Not silencing the ambitious part or the frightened one, but getting them around the same table so that a decision comes from the whole of you rather than from whichever voice happens to be loudest today. Resolving inner conflict this way pairs naturally with knowing [your own compass of values](/blog/act-values-based-living).

If you are weighing up which kind of support would fit, my piece on [the differences between counselling, therapy and coaching](/blog/counselling-vs-therapy-vs-coaching) may help clarify things, and the [frequently asked questions](/faq) cover the practicalities of how sessions work.
